summary: 1. High-stayed hooks (51-53% stayed) state a bold, direct, second-person reality or myth-bust in under 12 words ('Your eyes are leaking right now...'). 2. Low-stayed hooks (24-30% stayed) fail by using slow narrative scenario setups ('Your car swerves off...') or generic vague statements ('Most James Webb images hold secrets.'). 3. High-view topics center on personal body phenomena and iconic pop-culture science (eyes, onions, T. rex) rather than niche civil engineering (guardrail boxes). 4. Short, punchy titles asking a relatable question outperform formal scientific explanation titles. 5. While deep astronomy topics achieve high rewatch rates (167% avg view percentage), weak opening lines drop stayed_pct below 45%, preventing initial feed distribution.
winning_hooks: The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.
Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.
You are not sad when you chop an onion.
avoid: Narrative scenario setups that delay the core topic ('Your car swerves off the highway right toward...')
Generic claims with zero immediate stakes ('Most James Webb images hold secrets.')
Passive background facts before the plot twist ('Fossilized bones can last millions of years...')
next_experiment: Test a 1-second visual text overlay and hook change on a niche engineering video: Compare an indirect scenario opening vs. a direct myth-bust statement ('This steel box is designed to destroy your car safely').
